I think people may be jumping to conclusions in applying this to specific cases such as pharmaceuticals, climate change, or whatever else. Research and science in general has been experiencing an increasingly coercive influence driven by money. An increasing number of universities are applying ever more pressure on their researchers to produce big money grants and monetizable research. A now infamous incident was at Imperial College London. ICL is a generally well regarded research institution. However, they now openly require their researchers to generate 200,000 pounds or about $300,000 a year in research income.

One experienced and regarded researcher, Stefan Grimm, there was involved in research that wasn't pulling in huge grants. He was bullied and threatened over this. It ultimately drove him to suicide. This push towards money over quality means scientists and researchers are obligated to publish and pursue topics that generate funds. And people giving the big bucks want results which means the researchers also need to produce that, even when they may not necessarily exist.

This is dangerous on so many levels. So much of the science we rely on today relies on things that at one time would have been, at best, considered mental masturbation. For instance one field in mathematics is complex numbers which deals with the square root of negative numbers or imaginary numbers. This might seem useless, and at the time it was first being researched it probably was, but it's used extensively now. Every time a vehicle with 3 degrees of freedom moves (like an airplane or a space craft or probe), it's utilizing imaginary numbers, electrical engineering makes extensive use of imaginary numbers, quantum mechanics -which seems to be the next coming revolution in computing technology- relies heavily on them, and so on.

A journal like the Lancet at least acknowledging this is just huge and great news. But like they say, it's now a matter of taking that first step that nobody actually wants to.
